topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: AnySleep: a channel-agnostic deep learning system for high-resolution sleep staging in multi-center cohorts.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet studying its dynamics requires manual sleep staging, a labor-intensive step in research and clinical care. Across centers, polysomnography (PSG) recordings are traditionally scored in 30-s epochs for pragmatic, not physiological, reasons and vary in electrode count, montage, and subject characteristics. These constraints challenge harmonized multi-center studies and the discovery of robust biomarkers on shorter timescales. We present AnySleep, a deep neural network that scores sleep from any electroencephalography (EEG) or electrooculography (EOG) data at adjustable temporal resolutions. We trained and validated the model on over 20,000 overnight recordings (>200,000 h of EEG and EOG) from 28 datasets across multiple clinics to promote robust generalization across sites. The model attains state-of-the-art performance and surpasses or equals established baselines at 30-s epochs. Performance improves with more channels, yet remains strong when EOG is absent, or only EOG or single EEG derivations (frontal, central, or occipital) are available. On sub-30-s timescales, the model captures short wake intrusions consistent with arousals and improves the prediction of pathophysiological conditions (obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, insomnia) over 30-s scoring. We make the model publicly available to facilitate large-scale studies with heterogeneous electrode setups and accelerate biomarker discovery in sleep.

ai.topic: Channel-agnostic deep sleep staging
ai.reason: Channel-agnostic high-resolution sleep staging trained across 28 cohorts directly addresses generalization, signal variability, and sleep-staging core interests, with a broadly transferable methodological idea.
ai.summary: Developed AnySleep, a channel-agnostic deep neural network trained on over 20,000 overnight EEG/EOG recordings from 28 datasets to perform sleep staging at adjustable temporal resolutions. The model achieved state-of-the-art 30-s epoch performance, remained robust with limited channels, and at sub-30-s resolution improved prediction of obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, and insomnia compared to 30-s scoring.

papers.title: An automated EEG-ECG framework for CAP-HRV analysis: enabling brain-heart coupling studies in sleep disorders.
papers.abstract: Multimodal sleep analysis typically requires separate processing pipelines for electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG), which complicates joint investigation of sleep microstructure and autonomic regulation. Cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) scoring and heart rate variability (HRV) analysis are routinely performed in different software environments, limiting temporal alignment, reproducibility, and scalability. We present an open-source MATLAB framework that integrates rule-based CAP A1 detection and HRV feature extraction within a single, time-synchronized workflow. The pipeline performs standardized EEG and ECG preprocessing, rule-based CAP A1 detection during slow-wave sleep (SWS) implementing the Terzano scoring criteria, R-peak detection via the Pan-Tompkins algorithm, and computation of time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear HRV features by calling the open-source PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly. CAP annotations are aligned with 5-minute ECG epochs through the shared polysomnography (PSG) time base. The complete code is released as an open-source repository to support reuse and extension. Because HRV features are computed by calling the PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly, the pipeline introduces no reimplemented HRV routine and inherits that toolbox's validated feature definitions. CAP A1 detection is provided as a rule-based implementation of published criteria and has not yet been benchmarked against expert manual scoring. A worked example on the OSAD+ subgroup (n = 18) demonstrates pipeline output across CAP and non-CAP epochs, and a healthy-sleep A1-event HRV reference is reported from the public CAP Sleep Database (15 controls, 785 A1 epochs) as a descriptive cross-database reference. The framework provides a reproducible, rule-based, and modular tool for integrated EEG-ECG analysis of sleep microstructure and autonomic dynamics. By enabling synchronized CAP-HRV feature extraction in a single environment, it lowers the engineering barrier to brain-heart coupling research during sleep and provides a foundation for future extensions, including validated CAP detection, a matched-control study, a Python port, and cloud-based deployment.

ai.summary: Presented an open-source MATLAB framework integrating rule-based cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) A1 detection from EEG with heart rate variability (HRV) feature extraction from ECG within a time-synchronized workflow, using validated PhysioZoo/mhrv routines. A worked example on OSAD+ patients (n=18) and a healthy reference dataset (15 controls, 785 A1 epochs) demonstrated synchronized CAP-HRV output to facilitate brain-heart coupling research in sleep disorders.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Machine Learning for Biosignal Applications - A Review.
papers.abstract: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) has gained traction in an attempt to improve the interpretability and robustness of machine learning predictions. Specifically (medical) biosignals such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), electrooculography (EOG), and electromyography (EMG) could benefit from good UQ, since these suffer from a poor signal-to-noise ratio, and good human interpretability is pivotal for medical applications. To determine how uncertainty estimation can be used for biosignal tasks, we investigate current methods, use cases, applications, evaluations, and uncertainty measures. In this paper, we systematically review the state of the art of applying Uncertainty Quantification to Machine Learning tasks in the biosignal domain. All works from Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE XPlore and PsycINFO that discuss uncertainty in Machine Learning on one of the aforementioned biosignals is included. We present various methods, shortcomings, uncertainty measures and theoretical frameworks that currently exist in this application domain based on the 53 reviewed papers and related literature. We address misconceptions in the field, provide recommendations for future work, and discuss gaps in the literature in relation to diagnostic implementations as well as control for prostheses or brain-computer interfaces. Overall it can be concluded that promising UQ methods are available, but that research is needed on how people and systems may interact with an uncertainty-model in a (clinical) environment.

ai.topic: Uncertainty quantification for biosignals
ai.reason: Systematic review of UQ for EEG/ECG/EOG/EMG is highly transferable to interpretability, robustness, and calibration concerns for lightweight neural-signal methods.
ai.summary: Systematically reviewed 53 papers on uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for machine learning applied to biosignals such as EEG, ECG, EOG, and EMG. The review catalogued methods, evaluation measures, theoretical frameworks, and misconceptions, concluding that promising UQ approaches exist but that research on human-system interaction with uncertainty models in clinical settings is still needed.

papers.title: Automated attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder detection using an explainable EEGNet model based on electroencephalogram signals.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition where traditional diagnostics often suffer from subjective biases and a lack of objective biomarkers. In this study, we developed a novel, automated, and interpretable diagnostic framework using the specialized EEGNet model to extract spatio-temporal patterns directly from raw EEG signals, ensuring robust ADHD detection and model generalizability across a clinical lifespan ranging from 5 to 89 years. The primary innovation of this research lies in a specialized, lightweight EEGNet model that directly processes raw 5-second spatio-temporal EEG segments, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering or signal-to-image transformation. Our findings demonstrate that EEGNet achieves superior performance, reaching an average accuracy of 89.48% (±4.21%) and an AUC of 0.96 (±0.03), significantly outperforming the transfer learning models. A distinguishing feature of this work is the transition from black-box modeling to explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) by integrating Saliency Maps and SHAP values, which decoded the model's decision-making logic to identify key contributing channels (Fp1, Fp2, C3, T5, and A2) whose spatial attributions align with established neuroscientific literature on ADHD. The high ranking of the Fp1 (prefrontal) channel aligns with established neuroscientific evidence regarding executive dysfunction in ADHD. Furthermore, the implementation of a rigorous inter-subject evaluation demonstrates the preliminary clinical feasibility of this interpretable framework, providing a foundation for future validation on larger multi-center cohorts and offering a robust assistive tool for real-world neurological assessments.

ai.reason: Specialized lightweight EEGNet directly on raw EEG with XAI (saliency/SHAP) is a CPU-friendly, interpretable, transferable architecture analogous to state-classification needs, though ADHD-specific.
ai.summary: Developed a lightweight, explainable EEGNet model that processes raw 5-second spatio-temporal EEG segments for automated ADHD detection, achieving 89.48% (±4.21%) average accuracy and AUC 0.96 (±0.03), outperforming transfer learning models. Saliency maps and SHAP values identified key channels (Fp1, Fp2, C3, T5, A2) consistent with ADHD executive dysfunction literature.

papers.title: Decoding Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of qEEG biomarkers across clinical domains.
papers.abstract: This systematic review synthesized evidence on quantitative EEG (qEEG) correlates of Parkinson's disease (PD) across five domains: cognition, motor function, pharmacological interventions, neuromodulation, and sleep/non-motor features, evaluating qEEG's potential as a biomarker across these clinical domains. Following PRISMA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published from 1991 to 2025. We included studies with ≥10 idiopathic PD patients, resting-state qEEG, and empirical data. Methodological quality was assessed using JBI checklists and AMSTAR. We included 89 studies. Spectral slowing - reduced posterior dominant frequency and increased theta power - was the most consistent correlate of cognitive impairment. Connectivity measures (PLV, graph metrics) showed stronger associations with motor dysfunction, gait impairment, and freezing than spectral power alone. qEEG changed with dopaminergic drugs (increased alpha/beta) and neuromodulation (DBS, tDCS, rTMS, neurofeedback). Sleep studies revealed spindle density reductions linked to dementia risk. qEEG is a promising biomarker for PD, with distinct electrophysiological correlates across cognitive, motor, pharmacological, and neuromodulatory domains. However, methodological standardization is needed before clinical use. With standardized protocols and multicenter validation, qEEG could aid diagnosis, progression tracking, and personalized therapy in PD.

ai.topic: qEEG biomarkers systematic review in Parkinson's

ai.summary: Systematic review (PRISMA, 89 studies) synthesizing quantitative EEG correlates of Parkinson's disease across cognition, motor function, pharmacology, neuromodulation, and sleep. Spectral slowing (reduced posterior dominant frequency, increased theta) was the most consistent cognitive correlate, while connectivity measures better tracked motor dysfunction, and qEEG changed with dopaminergic drugs and neuromodulation.

papers.title: Interbrain synchrony analysis for fNIRS: A signal processing primer.
papers.abstract: Interbrain synchrony (IBS), also referred to as interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), has become a central construct in social neuroscience and beyond. It describes the temporal alignment of neural activity across individuals and has been studied in a range of paradigms, including sequential interactions, shared-stimulus settings, and hyperscanning, that is, the simultaneous neuroimaging of two or more individuals during real-time interaction. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is increasingly used for such studies because it supports portable, naturalistic, face-to-face paradigms. A central goal in these experiments is to quantify IBS between interacting individuals. Wavelet transform coherence (WTC) has become the most widely used method for estimating IBS in fNIRS studies. However, its application involves several non-trivial signal-processing assumptions and time-frequency trade-offs that are often not explicitly addressed, making it difficult to apply and interpret the method consistently. Reliable estimation of IBS is crucial not only for experimental design but also for the interpretation and comparison of results within and across studies. Here, we aim to support this endeavor by providing a principled overview of the relevant signal-processing foundations. To enable researchers to make informed methodological choices, the paper first introduces key concepts in time-frequency analysis and clarifies their relation to WTC. These principles are then connected to the analysis of IBS in fNIRS datasets, with particular emphasis on the time-frequency constraints inherent to wavelet-based methods. Building on these foundations, we provide practical recommendations for experiment design, preprocessing, and frequency targeting. By making resolution limits and analysis assumptions explicit, this primer aims to support improved study planning and more consistent interpretation of IBS in the rapidly growing field of fNIRS-based investigations and beyond. Establishing a shared methodological foundation for IBS analysis is essential for advancing toward more rigorous, transparent, and reproducible measurement of interpersonal brain dynamics in naturalistic neuroscience.

ai.topic: fNIRS interbrain synchrony signal-processing primer
ai.reason: Methodological primer on wavelet coherence and time-frequency trade-offs; signal-processing guidance is transferable even though modality is fNIRS, not EEG/animal sleep.
ai.summary: Methodological primer on quantifying interbrain synchrony (IBS) in fNIRS hyperscanning studies, explaining time-frequency analysis foundations underlying wavelet transform coherence and its resolution limits. Provides practical recommendations for experiment design, preprocessing, and frequency targeting to improve consistency and reproducibility of IBS measurement.

papers.title: Cortical traveling wave analysis reveals weaker resting forward theta waves and greater task-related modulation in obsessive compulsive disorder.
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with abnormalities in large-scale brain network dynamics. Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) captures local oscillatory activity but does not characterize spatiotemporal propagation patterns. This study investigates cortical traveling waves, which index directional information flow across the cortex, to determine whether they provide novel insights into altered neural communication in OCD. Resting-state (eyes-closed) and task-based (Go/NoGo, Flanker) EEG were recorded from 25 individuals with OCD and 27 healthy controls (HCs). Traveling waves were quantified along midline electrodes using two-dimensional Fast Fourier Transforms to extract forward (posterior-to-anterior) and backward (anterior-to-posterior) propagation in theta (4-8Hz) and alpha (8-13Hz) bands. Group differences were assessed using Bayesian and frequentist linear mixed-effects models controlling for age and sex. At rest, a significant group-by-direction interaction was observed in the theta band (P = 0.0006), driven by weaker forward traveling wave strength in OCD relative to HC. No group differences were observed for backward waves or in the alpha band. During the Flanker task, the OCD group showed a significantly greater increase in forward theta wave strength from rest than HC (P = 0.022). No associations were found between traveling wave measures and symptom severity. OCD is characterized by altered theta-band traveling wave dynamics, specifically reduced forward (bottom-up) signaling at rest, and increased task-related modulation during the Flanker task. These findings suggest disrupted hierarchical cortical communication and inefficient engagement of sensory-driven processes. The absence of symptom correlations suggests a potential trait-like neurophysiological marker or endophenotype of OCD.

ai.summary: Compared cortical traveling wave dynamics in 25 OCD patients and 27 controls using resting and task (Go/NoGo, Flanker) EEG, finding weaker resting forward theta traveling waves in OCD and greater task-related forward theta modulation during the Flanker task, with no associations to symptom severity. Findings suggest disrupted hierarchical cortical communication as a potential trait-like marker of OCD.

papers.title: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
papers.abstract: Early-stage brain injury encompasses subtypes such as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), silent stroke and subclinical brain injury. It is characterised by negative imaging findings, subtle symptoms and a high risk of long-term neurological deficits, presenting a key challenge in the early screening and prevention of neurological diseases. Traditional imaging techniques, such as structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT), can only identify organic morphological lesions. Their detection rate for early micro-injuries at the level of neuronal electrophysiology and brain network function is extremely low. Consequently, these techniques struggle to meet the clinical needs for early screening, assessment, and intervention. Electroencephalography (EEG) spectral changes (including conventional spectral slowing and 1/f aperiodic abnormalities) and large-scale dynamic neural network disruption across the entire brain are core pathological features of early brain functional damage; they may serve as indirect correlates of microscopic pathological changes such as an imbalance in neuronal excitation-inhibition and abnormalities in the efficiency of brain information transmission. Based on this, this paper proposes a Dynamic-Spectral Coupling (DSC) framework, which proposes spectral abnormalities as a potential upstream mechanism associated with network reorganisation. Within this framework, this narrative review summarizes dynamic functional magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic fMRI), EEG spectral analysis and multimodal fusion technologies, with a particular focus on elucidating the coupling mechanisms between EEG periodic and 1/f aperiodic spectral parameters and dynamic brain network indicators. The review outlines the screening value and application advantages of multimodal fusion technologies in mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury and subclinical brain injury. Furthermore, the paper summarises the current limitations of these technologies in terms of clinical translation, methodology and database development. Taking into account the clinical needs of neurorehabilitation, it proposes future development directions, including the development of lightweight devices, AI-assisted diagnosis, the establishment of standardised analytical systems and the translation of precision rehabilitation. The aim is to provide technical guidance and theoretical support for screening, risk stratification and rehabilitation planning in early-stage brain injury, while acknowledging that clinical utility remains to be established.

Summarizes multimodal fusion technologies for mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury, and subclinical injury while noting that clinical utility remains to be established.

papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

ai.reason: Human iEEG study of oscillatory predictive routing; spectral power analysis methods are adjacent and transferable, but the contribution is cognitive neuroscience rather than tooling.
ai.summary: Using human intracranial EEG from seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm, the study tested predictive routing predictions by measuring theta, alpha-beta and high-gamma power during auditory deviance, multisensory integration and McGurk incongruence. Superior temporal cortex showed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power for auditory deviance and McGurk stimuli, whereas frontal areas showed the alpha-beta decrease without a high-gamma prediction error signal and instead a strong theta-band prediction error in the McGurk condition.

papers.title: Differential circadian time modulates of dentate gyrus and CA1 excitation-inhibition balance and seizure threshold.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate seizure threshold and neuronal excitability in epilepsy. Temporal lobe seizures tend to arise more frequently during the diurnal phase relative to the nocturnal phase, yet dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells display elevated intrinsic excitability and CA1 pyramidal neurons show enhanced synaptic excitability at night. Here, we used male adult ICR mice (8-10 weeks old) as experimental subjects. Systemic pilocarpine injection was applied to pharmacologically trigger acute seizures, while AAV (pAAV2/9-CaMKIIα-hChR2 (H134R) - EYFP) delivery followed by optogenetic stimulation (10 Hz, 20 ms pulse width, 5 mW 473 nm blue light) was implemented to evoke region-specific hippocampal seizures. Combining continuous video-electroencephalography (vEEG) recording, optogenetically induced seizure assays, mRNA sequencing, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, we investigated circadian modulation of neuronal excitability and seizure threshold within the DG and CA1 subfields of the hippocampus. Our results revealed divergent circadian regulation of seizure thresholds between the DG and CA1 regions. Notably, the diurnal-nocturnal seizure threshold pattern in CA1 recapitulated that seen in systemic pilocarpien-provoked seizure models. We further confirmed that circadian cycles exert distinct regulatory effects on excitatory/inhibitory synaptic transmission and the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal principal neurons in the DG and CA1. Collectively, this work highlights region-specific circadian control over seizure susceptibility and the brain excitation-inhibition balance. Elucidating circadian influences on hippocampal physiology and seizure threshold will improve the translational value of anti-epileptic therapies and guide time-stratified seizure intervention strategies.

ai.summary: Using video-EEG, optogenetic seizure induction, mRNA sequencing, and patch-clamp recording in mice, this study showed that circadian time differentially modulates seizure thresholds and excitation-inhibition balance in hippocampal dentate gyrus versus CA1, with CA1 diurnal-nocturnal seizure threshold patterns matching systemic pilocarpine-induced seizures.

papers.title: Hair-compatible adhesive hydrogel electrodes for electroencephalography-based cybersickness detection and closed-loop mitigation.
papers.abstract: Cybersickness develops dynamically during virtual reality (VR) exposure, creating a need for continuous electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring. However, wearable EEG remains limited by the difficulty of establishing low-impedance, conformal, and mechanically stable electrode-scalp interfaces on hair-covered skin, especially under sweating and head motion. Here, we report a shell-assisted adhesive hydrogel electrode that combines hair penetration with stable scalp adhesion for rapid EEG acquisition. Poly (3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-modified polydopamine particles (PDA/PEDOT) are incorporated into an adhesive hydrogel to achieve high conductivity, strong adhesion, and mechanical compliance while preserving PEDOT conductivity without poly (styrene sulfonate) incorporation or additional treatment. A flexible silicone shell guides the hydrogel through hair, prevents unwanted hydrogel-hair adhesion, and enables intimate scalp contact. The electrode achieves an EEG signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 11.66 dB, while motion-induced interference under sweating is only 22.8% of that observed with traditional wet electrodes. Integrated into a wearable headband, the system detects cybersickness with 92.5% accuracy and enables closed-loop noisy galvanic vestibular stimulation (nGVS), increasing users' tolerance time by 52.3%. This work provides a practical strategy for hair-compatible soft biointerfaces and wearable neurotechnology for immersive human-machine interaction.

ai.summary: The authors developed a shell-assisted adhesive hydrogel electrode incorporating PDA/PEDOT particles to achieve conformal, hair-penetrating EEG recording with high conductivity and stability under sweating and motion. The electrode achieved an EEG SNR of 11.66 dB, showed motion interference at 22.8% of that of traditional wet electrodes, and, integrated into a wearable headband, detected cybersickness with 92.5% accuracy and closed-loop nGVS increased tolerance time by 52.3%.

papers.title: Cerebellar Topological Alterations Across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum.
papers.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized as a network disconnection syndrome. Despite evidence implicating the cerebellum in cognitive network integration, its associated electrophysiological network topology dynamics across the AD continuum remain unexplored. Methods: We enrolled 34 healthy controls (HC), 40 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 30 AD patients in this study. Cortical and cerebellar signals were recorded with a whole-brain EEG cap, and weighted functional connectivity networks were constructed using the phase-locking value (PLV). Graph theory was used to analyze network topological metrics across the AD continuum, focusing on cerebellar nodes. Topological metrics were correlated with neuropsychological scores, and network-based statistics (NBS) identified differential connectivity patterns among groups. Results: Network changes were most prominent in the theta band, with additional alterations in the delta band. Both MCI and AD groups showed reduced small-world metrics, although small-world organization remained present. These groups also showed increased nodal centrality in the frontal, occipital and cerebellar regions (at CB1, CB2 and CBZ in MCI but only at CBZ in AD) but decreased in the central and temporal regions. NBS analysis identified selective theta-band reorganization of cerebello-cortical connectivity. An inverted U-shaped relationship was found between cerebellar nodal centrality and neuropsychological scale scores. Conclusions: The cerebellar theta rhythm may be a key pattern involved in cognitive processing, and the topological changes of the cortical-cerebellar network may represent candidate electrophysiological network markers across different AD stages. These markers may reflect stage-related differences in cerebellar function, shifting from compensation in MCI to decompensation in AD.

ai.topic: EEG graph-theory connectivity in Alzheimer's continuum
ai.reason: PLV connectivity and graph metrics across clinical groups; connectivity methods are adjacent but applied clinical-neuro content with limited methodological novelty.
ai.summary: This EEG study compared 34 healthy controls, 40 MCI patients and 30 Alzheimer's disease patients using phase-locking-value functional connectivity and graph theory to characterize cerebellar-cortical network topology across the AD continuum. Theta-band small-world metrics were reduced in MCI and AD, cerebellar nodal centrality showed an inverted U-shaped relationship with neuropsychological scores, and network-based statistics revealed selective theta-band cerebello-cortical reorganization.

papers.title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling
papers.abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.

ai.summary: This paper presents a BIDS-formatted multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset from 24 healthy adults with carbon wire loop artifact sensors, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling of 13 thought dimensions (468 ratings per participant), and mental health surveys across two days (~1.33 hours of simultaneous data per person).

papers.title: Machine Learning Classification of Bipolar Disorder Across Mood States Using Natural Language Processing and Speech Analysis: Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BP) affects 1% to 3% of adults worldwide, with diagnostic delays averaging 6 years and high initial misdiagnosis rates. The absence of objective diagnostic measures contributes to clinical uncertainty and suboptimal outcomes. This study aimed to (1) develop a machine learning model for BP diagnosis and mood state classification using linguistic and acoustic features, (2) identify features associated with different mood states by comparing each with healthy controls (HC), and (3) explore whether features distinguish between mood states within BP. We analyzed data prospectively collected over 7 years from 61 patients with BP and 99 HC across Japan. Speech samples were collected via semistructured interviews over 1 to 5 visits and analyzed cross-sectionally, using aggregated or single-visit observations per participant rather than within-person longitudinal modeling. We extracted 6373 acoustic features (openSMILE 3.0, ComParE 2016) and 211 linguistic features. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-regularized logistic regression with nested cross-validation and age- and sex-matched undersampling was used. Mood states were classified as depressive state (DS; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale-17 [HAMD-17] ≥8, Young Mania Rating Scale [YMRS] ≤7), state with manic/mixed symptoms (MS/MX; YMRS ≥8), or euthymic state (ES; HAMD-17 ≤7, YMRS ≤7). Seven classification tasks included BP vs HC, each mood state vs HC, and interstate comparisons. Feature importance was validated via permutation testing (P<.05). Medication sensitivity analyses were performed. The model achieved high discrimination for BP vs HC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]=0.916, 95% CI 0.854-0.958; sensitivity 0.933; specificity 0.859) and strong performance for mood states vs HC (AUC=0.805-0.874). Acoustic features comprised 96% to 98% of the features achieving statistical significance (P<.05), including mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, spectral characteristics, and voice quality measures, showing strong correlations with diagnostic probabilities (|ρ|=0.35-0.85) and symptom severity (HAMD-17: ρ=-0.51; YMRS: ρ=-0.37); 2 to 4 linguistic features per comparison also reached significance. With sample independence ensured for interstate comparisons, DS vs ES significantly exceeded chance (AUC=0.760, permutation P=.03), whereas MS/MX vs ES (AUC=0.601, P=.20) and DS vs MS/MX (AUC=0.569, P=.30) did not, suggesting that markers primarily reflect persistent disease characteristics with partial state-associated components in depressive states. The combined acoustic-linguistic model, driven primarily by acoustic features, shows potential as an objective aid for BP diagnosis (AUC>0.9), largely free of medication confounding; some features remained detectable during euthymia, although ES discrimination could not be fully separated from concurrent antipsychotic treatment. Although DS showed partial distinguishability from ES, overall limitations remain for monitoring mood state changes. Findings require validation in diverse populations and against other psychiatric conditions.
keywords: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator

ai.topic: Speech-based ML classification of bipolar disorder

ai.summary: This observational study used LASSO-regularized logistic regression on 6373 acoustic and 211 linguistic features from speech samples of 61 bipolar disorder patients and 99 healthy controls to classify bipolar disorder and mood states. The model discriminated bipolar disorder from controls with AUC 0.916 and mood states from controls with AUC 0.805-0.874, with acoustic features comprising 96%-98% of significant features, while depressive vs euthymic state exceeded chance (AUC 0.760) and other interstate comparisons did not.

papers.title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study
papers.abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-unique predictive information in superior temporal regions and a separate frontal-pole interaction, Follower-unique predictive information in insular and superior frontal regions, sparse Synergy in the right rostral anterior cingulate cortex, and Redundancy spanning multiple cortical regions. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides a scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.

papers.title: Neurodynamical heterogeneous spiking neural network for spatiotemporal cognitive signal processing.
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) enable low-power brain-inspired computing via sparse binary spike transmission. Nevertheless, conventional homogeneous SNNs built exclusively upon leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons exhibit limited capacity for complex multi-scale temporal cognitive dynamics. Existing parametric-heterogeneous SNNs only tune internal hyperparameters within single-compartment LIF units and cannot capture diverse neuronal computations observed in biological circuits. Drawing inspiration from cross-neuronal dynamical heterogeneity in neural systems for multi-dimensional perception and cognition, this work proposes the Neurodynamical Heterogeneous Spiking Neural Network (NHSNN). NHSNN integrates three functionally distinct spiking neuron models: LIF, dendrite-inspired Pinsky-Rinzel (PR), and leaky resonate-and-fire (LRF), with each neuron type strategically assigned to dedicated functional modules to realise cross-neuronal heterogeneous spike encoding. We evaluate NHSNN across three representative cognitive-signal modalities: clinical electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, rhythmic auditory music data, and textual semantic sequences. On EEG-diagnosis and music-classification benchmarks, NHSNN achieves accuracy on a comparable scale relative to mainstream full-precision artificial neural networks (ANNs), though cross-study comparisons require caution owing to differing experimental protocols; on textual semantic tasks, it obtains accuracy comparable to existing SNN alternatives. Under matched network dimensionality, our approach substantially reduces parameter overhead while preserving intrinsic spike-driven energy advantages. Ablation and controlled baseline experiments verify that complementary cross-neuronal dynamical synergy - rather than raw increase of model complexity - yields strong multi-modal representations and removes requirements for heavy auxiliary modules. By balancing biological inspiration, temporal modeling capacity and computational efficiency, NHSNN provides a lightweight neuromorphic paradigm for resource-constrained edge cognitive-computing scenarios.

Evaluated on EEG diagnosis, music classification and textual semantic tasks, NHSNN reached accuracy comparable to mainstream full-precision ANNs on EEG and music benchmarks and comparable to existing SNN alternatives on text, with substantially reduced parameter overhead.

papers.title: A non-randomized trial of the effects of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation on cognitive performance and resting state connectivity.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has shown promise for enhancing cognition and emotion regulation. To date, most human studies have focused on narrow learning paradigms that limit our understanding of how taVNS influences complex, integrative cognitive operations. Moreover, the underlying mechanisms of taVNS are still not well understood. Building on preclinical findings that vagus nerve stimulation enhances cognitive flexibility and memory in animal models, this study investigated whether acute taVNS can modulate executive function and neural connectivity in healthy adults. Using a quasi-experimental design, forty healthy participants received either active or sham taVNS while completing executive function tasks and adaptive cognitive training (BrainHQ). High-density electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded during stimulation to assess cortical activity and functional connectivity across frequency bands. Multivariate analyses demonstrated significant effects of taVNS on cognitive function and EEG. Post-hoc group comparisons showed that compared to sham stimulation, active taVNS was associated with improved BrainHQ performance and decreased delta-band connectivity in left frontal, central, and parietal regions. Delta-band connectivity during active taVNS was positively associated with pre-to-post improvements in mood. No difference in executive function tasks was found between active and sham taVNS. Sensitivity analyses using adjusted models showed that these effects were sensitive to age, sex, and education. By evaluating multiple dimensions of executive function, these exploratory findings suggest that active taVNS may influence selected aspects of executive performance and frontal-parietal delta connectivity, potentially reflecting enhanced neural efficiency arising from the interaction between vagally mediated neuromodulation and continuously adaptive cognitive demands. However, these effects did not survive multiple-comparison correction and should therefore be interpreted cautiously and replicated in larger, prospectively powered studies.

papers.title: Case Report: Electroencephalography-informed low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the supplementary motor area in severe functional movement disorder.
papers.abstract: Functional movement disorder (FMD) is increasingly being recognized as a condition associated with abnormal brain network connectivity; however, effective treatment strategies remain limited. We report the case of a patient with severe FMD that developed following an occupational injury and was characterized by functional tremors accompanied by migraines and prominent autonomic symptoms. Based on electroencephalography (EEG) network analysis, low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the supplementary motor area was administered, followed by staged rehabilitation incorporating visual feedback. The combined intervention reduced tremors and improved gait speed, activities of daily living, and EEG network connectivity. This case highlights the potential utility of combining EEG-guided neuromodulation with staged rehabilitation for the treatment of FMD and supports further investigation of this approach.

papers.title: Effects of primary somatosensory cortex high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation combined with core stability training on pain and glutamate levels and neuromuscular function in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) involves pain-related changes in sensory processing, motor control, and broader neurobiological function. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is a relevant neuromodulation target because it contributes to sensory-discriminative pain processing and exhibits maladaptive plasticity in chronic pain states. However, S1-targeted high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) has been insufficiently studied in CLBP. To determine whether S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP, and to explore associated changes in paraspinal muscle biomechanical properties, resting-state EEG activity, and serum metabolites. In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 36 adults with CLBP received active or sham S1 HD-tDCS combined with a standardized 4-week core stability training program. Pain-related scale was assessed using the VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ. Secondary outcomes included biomechanical properties of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus measured using MyotonPRO. Exploratory outcomes included resting-state electroencephalographic alpha-band power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) connectivity, as well as untargeted serum metabolomics in a subset of participants. Compared with sham stimulation, active S1 HD-tDCS was associated with greater reductions in VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ scores after treatment. The active group also showed larger decreases in lumbar erector spinae and multifidus tone and stiffness, along with greater improvement in elasticity. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased alpha-band PSD across frontal, central, and parieto-occipital regions and reduced alpha-band PLV connectivity after active stimulation. In the metabolomics subset, active treatment was associated with greater reductions in circulating L-glutamate and enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways. Changes in pain intensity were correlated with changes in paraspinal muscle stiffness, central alpha-band PSD, and L-glutamate levels. S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training may improve short-term pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP. The accompanying muscular, electrophysiological, and metabolomic findings were consistent with the clinical changes. These findings support S1-targeted HD-tDCS as a potential adjunct to exercise-based rehabilitation in CLBP. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076620 (Registration date 2023-10-13).

papers.title: Impaired brain reserve is associated with increased risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy occurrence in patients with cirrhosis.
papers.abstract: Overt hepatic encephalopathy (OHE) is a severe complication of liver cirrhosis, independently associated with a poor outcome and subsequent cognitive impairment, which are often, but not always, related to covert hepatic encephalopathy (CHE). Brain reserve, reflecting overall brain health, may be reduced in patients with cirrhosis because liver disease and brain disorders share several risk factors. Patients with impaired brain reserve may display cognitive impairments that differ from those observed in CHE. We hypothesize that brain reserve could influence OHE occurrence. Retrospective study of a prospective cohort of outpatients with cirrhosis (from March 2018 to June 2024) referred for cognitive complaints, generally in the setting of a pre-TIPS or pre-transplant evaluation. A multimodal evaluation was conducted, including a clinical evaluation, blood sampling including ammonia level, complete neuropsychological testing, electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging with spectroscopy (MRS). The diagnosis of CHE was established by an adjudication committee based on this multimodal evaluation. History of OHE (HOHE) was collected retrospectively, and OHE occurrence was assessed prospectively. A total of 164 patients were included. The median age was 62 years [55-67], 72% were male, risk factors for cirrhosis were alcohol/ metabolic factors/viral for 65/52/14% of them. Median MELD was 12 [9-15] and Child Pugh index 8 [6-9]. Overall, 67% had a history of OHE and 66% were diagnosed with CHE according to the adjudication committee. Patients with HOHE displayed more brain atrophy at MRI (p = 0.045). During the one-year follow-up, a total of 48 patients developed OHE. In multivariate Fine and Gray competing risk analysis, brain atrophy (sHR = 4.80 [1.31 - 17.60], p = 0.018) and impaired memory evaluated by the FCSRT (sHR = 0.86 [0.79 - 0.94], p < 0.001) were independently associated with OHE occurrence, alongside with HOHE (sHR = 3.37 [1.14 - 9.99], p = 0.028), baseline MELD score (sHR = 1.21 [1.09 - 1.34], p < 0.001), EEG Background rhythm (sHR = 0.71 [0.50 - 1.00], p = 0.048) but not ammonia level (p = 0.057). Memory impairment and brain atrophy, which reflect an impaired brain reserve, are independently associated with OHE occurrence in patients with cirrhosis for CHE suspicion. Our results suggest that an impaired brain reserve is associated with increased risk of OHE occurrence in patients with cirrhosis.

The authors conclude that impaired brain reserve is associated with increased risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy.

papers.title: Neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) is the standard of care for moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy (NE). Although some centers consider TH for mild NE, neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants who do not meet eligibility criteria are incompletely defined. Infants evaluated for TH based on perinatal risk factors, but who did not meet institutional eligibility criteria, were prospectively enrolled. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months. Bayley-4 scores <85 were classified as sub-normative performance. Of 39 infants enrolled, 26 completed Bayley-4 assessments. Thirteen (50%) demonstrated sub-normative performance in at least one developmental domain; only one of them had an acute brain injury on MRI. Compared with infants with average-range performance, those with sub-normative performance had higher postnatal base deficits (10.1 vs 6 mmol/L, p 0.04), higher postnatal lactate levels (9.4 vs 4.9 mmol/L, p 0.05), and a trend toward less sleep-wake cycling on aEEG (45% vs 83%, p 0.06). A substantial proportion of infants evaluated for but not treated with TH demonstrated sub-normative developmental performance at 2 years. Absence of acute MRI-detected injury does not preclude later developmental vulnerability. These findings support longitudinal follow-up of infants who are evaluated for TH but do not meet TH criteria. Infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia demonstrated a measurable risk of neurodevelopmental vulnerability at 2 years, with 50% demonstrating sub-normative performance (>1 SD below the normative mean) in at least one domain on the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development Fourth Edition. Early postnatal metabolic abnormalities in infants evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia showed a potential association with later developmental outcomes. There is a need for improved risk stratification and structured longitudinal follow-up for infants evaluated for but who do not meet cooling criteria.

Higher postnatal base deficits and lactate levels, and a trend toward less sleep-wake cycling on aEEG, were observed in those with sub-normative performance.

papers.title: Metabolic Imaging of Optic Nerve Oligodendrocytes Following AAV-Mediated Sensor Delivery.
papers.abstract: Oligodendrocytes are key regulators of white matter integrity, supporting rapid nerve conduction and sustaining axonal health. They engage in metabolic interactions with axons, yet their metabolic dynamics and specializations remain difficult to study in intact tissue. The optic nerve provides an accessible and well-structured white matter tract in which oligodendrocytes maintain their native association with axons and surrounding glia. Here, we present a protocol for targeted biosensor expression in oligodendrocytes of the optic nerve using intracerebroventricular injection of adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) at postnatal day 10 (P10). This approach enables imaging of oligodendrocyte metabolism in an intact 3D environment. As a use case, we demonstrate expression and application of a genetically encoded glucose sensor, allowing metabolic imaging to be combined with functional assays such as optic nerve electrophysiology. This method provides a flexible platform for studying oligodendrocyte physiology and metabolic adaptation in health and disease.

papers.title: Case Report: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease initially misdiagnosed as ischemic stroke: a diagnostic challenge and biomarker-based clarification.
papers.abstract: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) is a rare and uniformly fatal prion disorder characterized by rapidly progressive dementia and heterogeneous neurological manifestations. Early sCJD may be misinterpreted as cerebrovascular disease, particularly when focal neurological deficits, unilateral diffusion abnormalities, and vascular risk factors coexist. We report a 76-year-old man with a history of hypertension who initially presented with dizziness and gait instability, followed by progressive right-sided weakness, and was initially diagnosed with ischemic stroke in the setting of intracranial arterial stenosis. Despite antiplatelet and vascular management, the patient experienced rapid cognitive decline, psychiatric disturbances, aphasia, and progressive hemiparesis. Follow-up MRI demonstrated progressive, non-territorial cortical ribbon-like diffusion restriction predominantly involving the left insular, parietal, frontal, and temporal cortices. CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated total tau (4553.50 pg/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 399 pg/mL), phosphorylated tau (66.93 pg/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 50 pg/mL), and 14-3-3γ protein (50515 AU/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 20,000 AU/mL). Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies and metagenomic next-generation sequencing were negative. PRNP genetic testing detected no pathogenic variant in the patient and his son. EEG showed diffuse slowing without periodic sharp wave complexes. According to the 2017 International CJD Surveillance Network criteria, the diagnosis was classified as probable sCJD on the basis of rapidly progressive cognitive impairment, two clinical features (documented cerebellar ataxia and pyramidal signs), characteristic MRI abnormalities, and positive CSF 14-3-3; the typical EEG criterion was absent and RT-QuIC was not performed. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of early sCJD initially misdiagnosed as ischemic stroke in the presence of coexisting vascular pathology. Recognition of non-vascular diffusion patterns, careful reassessment of atypical clinical progression, and adjunctive CSF biomarker assessment may facilitate timely diagnostic reconsideration and help avoid unnecessary interventions.

The case highlights non-vascular diffusion patterns and CSF biomarkers as aids to diagnostic reconsideration.

papers.title: The History of Child Neurology in Iran: From Ancient Times to the Present.
papers.abstract: To describe the historical development of child neurology in Iran, from early Persian-Islamic medical concepts of neurological disease to contemporary subspecialty practice, education, research, and service delivery. This narrative historical review synthesized accessible peer-reviewed publications, institutional histories, university and hospital documents, professional-society resources, and publicly available records concerning Persian medical scholarship, medical education, pediatric hospitals, subspecialty training, neonatal care, epilepsy services, newborn screening, and neurogenetics in Iran. When historical dates or attributions were inconsistent, they were interpreted cautiously and reported as approximate or unspecified. Early Persian and Islamic medical traditions, including the works associated with Rhazes, Avicenna, and Jorjani, documented observations relevant to seizures, paralysis, developmental disorders, and cranial nerve function, although child neurology was not yet a distinct specialty. Modern development was facilitated by nineteenth-century educational reform, especially Dar al-Funun, followed by the establishment of pediatric teaching and referral hospitals, including Bahrami Children's Hospital, Children's Medical Center, and Mofid Children's Hospital. Integration of medical education and health services after 1985 strengthened specialty training and referral systems. Contemporary child neurology includes structured two-year subspecialty training, pediatric clinical neurophysiology and epilepsy fellowship programs, long-term video-electroencephalography monitoring, epilepsy monitoring units, neonatal intensive care expansion, newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism and phenylketonuria, neurogenetic resources such as Iranome, dedicated research centers, and an indexed specialty journal. Persistent challenges include uneven regional access, economic constraints, sanctions-related procurement barriers, and workforce migration. Child neurology in Iran has evolved from descriptive neurological knowledge embedded in Persian-Islamic medicine into a hospital-based, research-oriented pediatric subspecialty. Future progress depends on retaining the specialist workforce, strengthening provincial referral pathways, expanding registries and genomic capacity, and improving resilience of clinical and research infrastructure.

It identifies persistent challenges including uneven regional access, sanctions-related procurement barriers, and workforce migration.

papers.title: Reported Life-Threatening Polymorphic Ventricular Arrhythmia With Torsade-Like Morphology in a Patient With Gordon Syndrome and Hyperkalaemia.
papers.abstract: Gordon's syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type II) is a rare, inherited tubulopathy characterised by salt-sensitive hypertension, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis despite preserved renal function. Pathogenic variants affecting the with-no-lysine (K) signalling pathway include WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3. We report the case of a 37-year-old woman with genetically confirmed CUL3-related Gordon's syndrome who developed hyperkalaemia after a three-week interruption of bendroflumethiazide. During pre-hospital assessment, ambulance clinicians documented a self-terminating rhythm that they identified as torsade de pointes. The original recording cannot be retrieved; consequently, the rhythm classification, preceding QT interval, and possible alternative rhythm or artefact could not be independently assessed. Point-of-care venous blood gas potassium was 4.8 mmol/L, whereas formal laboratory potassium was 6.1 mmol/L. The sampling and processing information available did not establish the cause of this discrepancy. Subsequent echocardiography, computed tomography coronary angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, and additional electrical assessment did not identify a definitive alternative substrate, although an intermittent electrical disorder could not be excluded. Following treatment of hyperkalaemia and multidisciplinary cardiology and electrophysiology review, an extravascular implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. Bendroflumethiazide was resumed, with subsequent improvement in potassium control. This case highlights the importance of uninterrupted thiazide therapy in Gordon's syndrome, assessment of discordant potassium measurements, and careful interpretation of a reported serious rhythm event when its original tracing is unavailable. The temporal association with hyperkalaemia does not establish that it caused torsade de pointes.

The authors note that the original rhythm tracing was unavailable and that the temporal association does not establish causation.

papers.title: Cre-loxP as an option in cardiovascular disease research.
papers.abstract: The Cre-LoxP system is based on site-specific recombination mediated by the enzyme Cre recombinase. This system allows spatiotemporal control of gene expression in inducible models by utilizing specific promoters or enhancers that direct the expression of Cre recombinase in particular tissues or as a response to external signals at a specific moment in the life of the model organism, such as drug administration. In cardiovascular research, the Cre-LoxP system has been fundamental in generating mouse models replicating specific human pathological conditions. A growing area of interest is the use of Cre-LoxP in optogenetics, where it allows the expression of light-sensitive ion channels to modulate the activity of specific tissues such as the heart. This approach provides new avenues for studying cardiac electrophysiology and developing targeted therapeutic strategies.
